To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

papers.title: Inspectable LLM-Simulated Participants for Qualitative Interview Rehearsal
papers.authors: Hangyue Zhang, Qiran Hu, Ziyi Zhang, Hyanghee Park et al.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used across research workflows, including research ideation, qualitative analysis, and participant simulation. Within work on participant simulation, prior studies have largely evaluated simulated participants by how realistic or human-like their responses appear, leaving less known about how researchers use and critique these materials when revising interview protocols before fieldwork. We present Rehearsim, an inspectable research probe that treats LLM-simulated participants as materials for methodological rehearsal rather than substitutes for human participants. Rehearsim combines literature-grounded participant construction, interactive interview rehearsal, and traceable thematic review while keeping protocol decisions under researcher control. In a study with 21 qualitative researchers, participants used simulated materials to surface assumptions and gaps, reconsider participant populations, revise target populations, and develop follow-up probes. They also identified risks, including the concealment of weak questions, dismissal of unexpected synthetic details, and interpretive anchoring from generated themes. We derive an inspectable-rehearsal framework emphasizing traceability, contestability, researcher control, and epistemic boundaries.

papers.title: Orchestrating Key Scarcity: Global Capacity Allocation in Hybrid QKD-PQC Networks
papers.authors: Pablo P. Rejo, Manuel Fernández-Veiga, Ana Fernández-Vilas, Diego Cajaraville-Aboy et al.
papers.summary: This article presents a Distributed Key Management System (DKMS) that provisions quantum-safe symmetric encryption keys to applications across a network. To overcome the distance and rate limitations inherent to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the architecture adopts a hybrid design: it utilizes multi-hop trusted relays for physical key transport, while applying an end-to-end Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) layer to ensure the relayed key material remains strictly protected from intermediate nodes. Because QKD transforms key generation into a scarce physical resource, managing unpredictable application demands poses a critical capacity allocation problem. The core contribution of this work is an SDN-driven control plane that globally orchestrates the network. Rather than relying on vulnerable hop-by-hop capacity reservations, a central controller simultaneously computes optimal filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers. This global orchestration ensures that no application is starved and that all key buffers synchronize their filling processes. Evaluated on a Kubernetes-based digital twin across five distinct network topologies, the controller successfully filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes. Furthermore, under deliberately excessive demand, the network demonstrated graceful degradation, safely rejecting excess requests through controlled rate-limiting rather than experiencing catastrophic failure.

papers.title: XRust: Detecting Logical Races in Rust Linux Drivers
papers.authors: Qingxiao Xu, Ze Sheng, Zhicheng Chen, Arjun Manikandan et al.
papers.summary: Rust is increasingly used in Linux to improve memory safety, but its guarantees do not prevent logical races: individually synchronized operations can still interleave in ways that violate higher-level invariants. Detecting such bugs typically requires manually written specifications and carefully controlled execution environments. We present XRust, a technique for detecting logical races in Linux Rust drivers without manually specified invariants. Using Logical Happens-Before (LHB) analysis, XRust identifies shared-state accesses relevant to logical ordering, automatically constructs operation-pair harnesses, and uses serial differential oracles to detect concurrent executions inconsistent with either serial order. XRust also uses lightweight userspace abstractions to execute driver code under reproducible schedules. Applied to Linux 7.3-rc2, XRust identifies 17 shared objects across 102 Rust files from ten drivers, constructs 1,654 executable harnesses, and discovers two previously unknown logical races. The rnull block-driver race has been confirmed by Linux maintainers, with a fix accepted into the Linux block subsystem tree.

papers.title: Detecting AI Training in Datacentre Power
papers.authors: Tom Kimpson, Mauricio Baker, Emlyn Graham
papers.summary: AI governance agreements require methods to detect large model training runs on a monitored computing cluster, without trusting the operator. We develop a method to detect synchronous model training in facility-level power by Viterbi tracking of the wandering iteration cadence. On simulated datacentre power, when the operator makes no attempt to hide, the Viterbi tracker detects at least 96% of training runs against a declared inference workload, at a 1% false-alarm rate and within 0.04 of the Neyman–Pearson optimum, given a meter that samples at 2 Hz or faster. Of eight adversarial strategies an operator might use to hide, only extreme variation of the work per iteration evades the tracker. Its strongest form hides training in up to 73% of five-minute observations, but over a day at least 87% of such runs are still caught, at a 0.1% false-alarm rate per run. This adversarial strategy costs no throughput, but in small-scale training the operator needs 93–267% more compute to reach the same loss. A modest passive meter is sufficient to make hidden training both detectable and expensive, which makes power metering a promising part of compute verification that does not depend on trusting the operator.

papers.title: RIPE Atlas Measurements and Geolocation Providers: A Longitudinal Consistency Evaluation
papers.authors: Jonatas Marques, Oliver Gasser
papers.summary: IP geolocation supports many Internet services and operations, including but not limited to content delivery, fraud detection, content localization, and regulatory compliance. However, assessing the reliability and accuracy of IP geolocation providers is challenging and only partially explored. In this paper, we present a longitudinal study evaluating the consistency between RIPE Atlas latency measurements and location estimates from four popular geoproviders as a proxy for geolocation quality. Analyzing six months of data we observe mostly stable consistency levels through time, with fluctuations largely related to changes to the mix of targets being measured by RIPE Atlas each day. We also observe that consistency levels can differ greatly between geoproviders, with IPinfo leading DB-IP (the next best) by 5.4 percentage points for IPv4 and 11.5 percentage points for IPv6. Finally, the analysis reveals distinct degradation patterns across providers for different subsets of IP addresses. For example, for IPv4 router addresses, MaxMind consistency is 10.7 percentage points worse than in the general case while IPinfo is only 1.6 percentage points worse; for IPv6, the pattern flips and routers are geolocated more consistently than non-routers by all providers.

papers.title: Quantum-Seeded Distributed Post-Quantum Group Signatures for 5G V2X Communications
papers.authors: P. Blanco-Casal, P. Rejo-Iglesias, D. Cajaraville-Aboy, J. Vecino-Peñas et al.
papers.summary: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications rely on elliptic-curve signatures that a quantum adversary breaks and on pseudonym certificates whose anonymity rests on rotation rate, not cryptography. This work presents qDGSP, a post-quantum V2X infrastructure: a hash-based dynamic group signature scheme (DGSP, over SPHINCS+ and WOTS+) distributed between a central controller and roadside verifiers. Group keys derive deterministically from quantum key distribution (QKD) seeds served over the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface, so no group-signature secret crosses the classical channel. qDGSP-EA (Ephemeral Association) binds an ephemeral ML-DSA-65 key to one group signature per 5G cell: messages remain unlinkable across cells, linkable within one. On a testbed with emulated 5G links, median end-to-end latency stayed within the 100ms ETSI budget for every variant. The qDGSP-EA intra-cell DENM matched the NIST ML-DSA-65 baseline on the wire, and under load EA mode raised delivery from roughly 78% to 93%.

papers.title: Design and Control of a Multimodal Legged-Aerial Robot Through Separate Control Contraction Metrics
papers.authors: Kaushik Venkatesh Krishnamurthy, Eric Sihite, Alireza Ramezani, Morteza Gharib
papers.summary: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.

papers.title: Scrambled Multiply-with-Carry Pseudorandom Number Generators
papers.authors: Sebastiano Vigna
papers.summary: Multiply-with-carry (MWC) generators are very fast pseudorandom number generators whose quality depends on the choice of a multiplier, and is usually assessed by applying the spectral test to an associated multiplicative congruential generator. We show that the special form of the modulus imposes structural limitations on the lattice structure of every MWC generator, which the generalized MWC generators of Goresky and Klapper mitigate; in our tests, xoring each output with its carry removes them. Since these limitations make the usual worst-case criterion useless, we rank candidates by a weighted geometric mean of their figures of merit, which does not depend on their normalization, and suggest multipliers for generators with 64 to 256 bits of state. Along the way, we correct some errors in the literature. In the end, we propose MWC192X, a 64-bit generator with 192 bits of state that passes all tests we are aware of, and emits an output in half a nanosecond.

papers.title: RadGeoLoc: Radar Geolocalization via Particle Filtering
papers.authors: Shaunak Kolhe, Peng Jiang, Kasi Viswanath, Srikanth Saripalli
papers.summary: In real-time autonomous field applications, GNSS is often unreliable and inaccurate. A possible solution is localizing against a prebuilt map like a satellite image, as it is georeferenced and already surveyed. In this work, we localize a spinning radar measurement against overhead RGB imagery with a learned observation model. We use a radar representation pretrained by masked reconstruction and align it to features from a satellite image. A particle filter propagated by radar odometry proposes candidate poses, and our observation model provides a likelihood over these poses. We evaluate our method over 31 distinct routes, over 8 datasets spanning both urban and offroad conditions using only ground radar and a coarse local prior. We also examine the robustness over changing weather using repeated traversals over the same route over 13 months, in both urban and offroad conditions.

papers.title: A Hybrid Information Flow Analysis Framework for Android Hybrid Apps
papers.authors: Jyoti Prakash, Mikkel Baun Kjærgaard, Abhishek Tiwari
papers.summary: The WebView interface in Android (hybrid) applications enables the native side (e.g., Java) to exchange data with the Web (e.g., JavaScript). This creates cross-language information flow channels that existing single-language analyzers cannot analyze. Existing hybrid app analyses address only part of the problem: some build bridge-aware call graphs but provide limited information-flow analysis, some rely on coarse assumptions, and some focus only on web vulnerabilities. We present MifDroid, a static-analysis- guided dynamic-analysis framework with a lifecycle-aware per-WebView call graph, a bridge-aware type-and-effect system, and a modular JavaScript analysis engine. We evaluated MifDroid on 338 apps from the F-Droid repository (out of 4,126 total) that use addJavascriptInterface, enabling active communication between Java and JavaScript. Our guided dynamic phase adds 662 entries to the 444 produced by static analysis, raising the resolution rate from 36.5% to 74.5%, produces the resolved bridge-related entries for 115 apps that static analysis leaves empty. MifDroid reported 14 vulnerable cross-language information flows, five of which have been accepted and fixed by the maintainers.

papers.title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Carson Sobolewski, Anjali Parashar, Fei Chen, Yingke Li et al.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution. Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and π0.5 in simulation and π0.5-DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.

papers.title: Certifying Repeatable Entry-Replay Witnesses for COBOL-to-Java Migration
papers.authors: Andras L. Ferenczi, Mariya Bessonov, Allwyn Ponnudurai, Chandrakanth R. Mamillapalli et al.
papers.summary: Producing synthetic data for comparison testing a migrated COBOL application is a major challenge that agentic migrations face today. Our prior paper, the Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration, presents a deterministic oracle to facilitate such migrations, the Locksmith Loop. We now propose a novel method for achieving high branch and paragraph coverage through generated synthetic end-to-end test cases, by means of entry-replay test-case certification by observing the code execution trace on a surrogate COBOL program that mocks external interactions via a chronological external-operation tape. We applied our method to a very large COBOL program with 33,429 lines of code to generate 849 synthetic end-to-end test cases covering 2,973/3,806 source branches (78.1%) and 989/1,033 main-AST paragraphs (95.7%). Using the Locksmith Loop's projected-agreement validation, the generated Java code matched the COBOL surrogate on the specified observations across all 849 certified synthetic end-to-end test cases. During the campaign we detected 61 defects and fixed the Java generator accordingly. To test whether the coding agent could silently introduce business logic bugs, we seeded 450 defects into the Java code, such as deleted writes, deleted paragraph calls, and altered rounding, to verify how many of these would be detected by the gating methodology. The gate detected 47.6%, including all deleted writes and paragraph calls in executed code, but was unable to detect the rounding and precision defects.

papers.title: The Differential Effects of AI Abstention on Advice Acceptance
papers.authors: Nicholas Wolczynski, Yotam Liel, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Lior Zalmanson
papers.summary: AI advising systems are typically designed to always provide a response. Recent work has focused on developing systems that withhold advice in some instances, such as when advice quality is questionable, to improve the overall quality of guidance when it is given; a design paradigm we refer to as AI abstention. While substantial work has focused on optimizing when models should abstain, little is known about how users respond to systems that abstain. In a preregistered experiment, participants made repeated financial decisions, assisted by one of two advising regimes: an AI that advises selectively or one that advises on every decision. We find that the same AI abstention regime produces differential effects depending on the user: it increases advice acceptance among users with high perceived expertise and tends to decrease it among users with low perceived expertise. This differential effect is accounted for by the cognitive burden users face when repeatedly reconciling AI recommendations with their own judgment; AI abstention appears to relieve this burden among users with high perceived expertise, and in doing so increases their receptivity to advice. Further, AI abstention mitigates the decline in advice acceptance observed among expert users over repeated interactions. Exploratory evidence also suggests it increases appropriate acceptance where advice would improve the decision, increasing the downstream accuracy of perceived experts. The AI abstention regime is thus a first-order design property of AI advisory systems, and one that must be calibrated to the users a system serves.

papers.title: Neural Controlled Directional Frame Generation for Sprite Animation
papers.authors: Kenneth Alonso, Gustavo Patow
papers.summary: Sprite-based animation remains prevalent in video game development, but production workflows require capabilities beyond traditional in-betweening. While existing neural interpolation methods can generate intermediate frames, animators also need forward extrapolation to predict motion continuations and backward extrapolation for editing and reverse-engineering existing sprite sheets. Current video generation models either operate on natural video content with stochastic diffusion sampling incompatible with production requirements, or focus exclusively on interpolation without addressing extrapolation tasks. We present a deep learning approach for controlled directional frame generation in sprite animation using three specialized expert models that share identical U-Net encoder-decoder architectures and several domain-specific modifications, including RGBA-aware processing, multi-scale flow refinement, pixel-shuffle upsampling, and alpha-gated blending. Each model is trained on different temporal orderings of the same curated dataset: previous (frames 2,3>1), middle (frames 1,3>2), and next (frames 1,2>3). We demonstrate that only 280 carefully curated sprite triplets enable effective training for all three directional tasks without requiring massive generic datasets. Evaluation on 42 test triplets using the FLIP metric shows that all three models achieve comparable quality–previous (0.26), middle (0.26), and next (0.27)–with no significant degradation for extrapolation versus interpolation, outperforming general-purpose baselines by 17-57%. With deterministic single-pass generation and compact model, our method provides the first practical solution for controllable any-position frame generation specifically tailored for pixel art sprite animation workflows, validating that quality-over-quantity data curation enables specialized deep learning for niche visual domains.

papers.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
papers.authors: Xiaohang Tang, Rehema Abulikemu, Peng Gao, Yan Chen
papers.summary: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.

papers.title: "It Wouldn't Have Been So Apparent to Me": Evaluating How Thought-Level Progress Tracking Supports Psychosocial Goals
papers.authors: Shiyu Xu, Ruishi Zou, Anna R. Van Meter, Addie Weaver et al.
papers.summary: We pursue psychosocial goals every day, from coping with anxiety, to pursuing personal growth. While prior research has designed systems for tracking progress towards behavioral goals, fewer studies have focused on progress towards psychosocial goals - and the thinking changes people make to address them. As a first step, we present Thought-GPS, a system that visualizes potential markers of such thought-level progress in-the-moment as users interact with an AI-supported cognitive restructuring intervention. We evaluated Thought-GPS through a mixed-methods single-session study with 30 participants, comparing Thought-GPS with an active control condition without progress markers. We found preliminary evidence that participants using Thought-GPS reported greater clarity about how they might change to pursue their goals, stronger motivation to reflect on goal progress, and greater engagement in that reflection. Participants also reported that progress markers made subtle progress visible, helped them engage in deeper reflection, and connect conversational insights to their personal goals.

papers.title: pyFDN: A Python Toolbox for Feedback Delay Network Design, Analysis, and Optimization
papers.authors: Sebastian J. Schlecht, Facundo Franchino, Jeremy B. Bai
papers.summary: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) provide a compact representation of recursive audio systems for artificial reverberation and decorrelation. Their practical use spans structured matrix design, acoustic decay shaping, numerical simulation, and modal analysis, increasingly combined with differentiable optimization. We present pyFDN, an open-source Python toolbox that brings these operations into a common workflow. The library combines numerical design and analysis routines with block-based time-domain processing and integration with FLAMO for frequency-domain differentiable processing. Explicit network builds and JSON presets connect design, optimization, rendering, and reuse. This paper describes the software architecture, representative capabilities, and reproducibility mechanisms of version 0.5.0, providing a reference for research and teaching that use the toolbox.

papers.title: Who Approved This? Coding Agents, Human Accounts, and Merge-Gate Evidence at a Fintech Startup
papers.authors: Adam Manji
papers.summary: From 3 October, every non-bot merge into our main branch passed a non-author review gate, yet 71 of those 263 merges (27%) rested only on an approval that a coding agent had submitted through the technical lead's GitHub account, and the platform recorded each one as an ordinary approval by the lead. We report twelve weeks of agent-driven development at Bashi AI, a fintech startup preparing for a SOC 2 audit: 786 merged pull requests, 657 of them associated with agents by explicit markers or by inference, analysed from platform records and saved agent-session transcripts. In the gated phase, an agent session submitted every approval the lead's account gave on a colleague's pull request, and issued nearly all of its merges; the records cannot show who decided any of them. We recompute, for every merge, a core gate property: a non-author approval and a passing required check, both before the merge and both on the exact revision merged. The recomputation confirmed the gate wherever branch protection applied and found where it did not: agents switching enforcement off around individual merges, a merge script that recorded failed checks as passing, and an agent collapsing a stack of pull requests through unprotected branches. The engineers' survey answers show that one engineer's approvals also rested on review agents, with the person validating findings and deciding, and both engineers say review mattered when it tested a change against something outside the diff. We draw lessons on recording decision authority separately from account identity, keeping agents' credentials away from the controls they operate under, and checking evidence at the branch and revision where integration happens.

papers.title: CanvasObs: Structured Spatial Observation for Agent Editing on 2D Infinite Canvases
papers.authors: Jiahao Xu, Haohui Wang, Rebecca Faust, Dawei Zhou et al.
papers.summary: Editing agents on 2D infinite canvases must reason about application state that pixels may not reveal. Targets may be offscreen or covered, while visual containment and touching arrows may disagree with recorded frame membership or connector bindings. We ask how a structured observation layer can support accurate object selection during agentic editing on 2D infinite canvases. We present CanvasObs, which augments visual context with a structured payload and guidance for reading four components: Identity & State, Visibility & Structure, Relations, and Offscreen Object bounds in action coordinates. A Remote Team Handoff case study illustrates retrieving an editable offscreen copy, choosing a covered chart by color, separating cards by frame membership, and preserving an evidence connection. We turn these cases into ten controlled configurations and compare CanvasObs with the baseline agent in 1,200 browser trials across three models. CanvasObs improves Correct target for every model. Combined across models, it raises Correct target from 16.5% to 48.3%, an increase of 31.8 percentage points (95% confidence interval [29.0, 34.7]), and Full task success from 4.3% to 25.0%. These results show that compact structured observation can improve object choice on 2D infinite canvases without redesigning the editing pipeline.

papers.title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
papers.authors: Kevin Pu, Anh Truong, Michael Terry, Carrie J. Cai et al.
papers.summary: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

papers.title: Disjoint in Name Only: Illusory Resilience in the Internet
papers.authors: Subhadeep Sahoo, Hrishikesh B Acharya
papers.summary: Internet path diversity is usually verified at the logical layer: two alternatives may share no AS or IP link yet traverse the same facility, conduit, or submarine landing zone. We call this gap illusory resilience and define the Illusory Resilience Index (IRI) as the latent hazard-weighted physical overlap of a logically disjoint path pair. To detect such hidden exposure without carrier underlay maps, we audit three public signals: correlated BGP withdrawals during documented physical incidents, operator interconnection-footprint overlap, and shared submarine landing zones. Two signals survive calibration; the 60-second BGP signal does not. Across 47 operators in ten regions, same-region pairs have substantially greater listed facility overlap than cross-region pairs, and one Marseille campus colocates 153 operator pairs. Across 68 cable systems in twelve corridors, 31-100% of candidate within-corridor pairs share a 25 km coastal hazard zone; two corridors are fully saturated, and the same rule recovers ten of eleven cable pairs documented as co-damaged in 2024. The rejected temporal predicate has a 0.444 null firing rate and no hits among twelve monitored positive pairs. Public data therefore expose substantial shared-risk structure behind nominal diversity and identify where stronger physical-path verification is warranted.

papers.title: Beyond Two Tracks: Speaker-Anchored Full-Duplex Dialogue Recovery
papers.authors: Yuxuan Chen, Yang Xiao, Jack Sun, Chak Sun et al.
papers.summary: Spoken interaction is moving from alternating turns to full-duplex conversation, where an agent listens while speaking. Learning this coordination requires natural dialogue with persistent speaker-resolved tracks, a data requirement that remains difficult to satisfy at scale. Generative recovery offers a route from ordinary recordings, but recovering two voices is not enough: their track assignments can drift as the conversation unfolds. We address this missing link with speaker-anchored routing before diffusion: a 1.84M-parameter module matches the separator's coarse streams to fixed enrollment identities and orders them before a frozen generator reconstructs the speech, without retraining the generator or altering the reconstructed audio. On 25-minute remote conversations, routing cuts wrong-track time from 43.9% to 4.1%, below the 6.2% of matched-enrollment waveform re-identification, with its largest advantage when one participant holds the floor (17.8% versus 28.6%), and raises fixed-track activity F1 from 0.46 to 0.84 while per-chunk reconstruction quality is unchanged. The same router transfers to unseen face-to-face and telephone recordings, and a margin-gated verification step brings their wrong-track time to 0.9-1.7% while embedding 20-36% of the output, where full re-identification embeds all of it. Recovered voices thus become the participant-consistent tracks that full-duplex dialogue modeling needs. Audio examples: https://elpsykongloo.github.io/beyond-two-tracks/

papers.title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Marcel Rogge, René Schuster, Didier Stricker
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.

papers.title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
papers.authors: Wenqian Zhang, Yangyi Huang, Zigeng Xu, Weiyang Liu et al.
papers.summary: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

papers.title: Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
papers.authors: Adar Elad, Gal Metzer, Omer Dahary, Min Lu et al.
papers.summary: A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

papers.title: FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances
papers.authors: Bandhan Patel, Sushruth Harsha, Kwangsung Oh, In Kee Kim
papers.summary: Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage. We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at 0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.

papers.title: MuLaCover: Flexible Cover Song Generation via Symbolic Tonal Control
papers.authors: Lynn Yi, Zihan Xiong, Junjie Cao, Xiaolong Weng et al.
papers.summary: A cover song re-renders an existing piece, most commonly by preserving its tonal content – melody and chord progression – while reshaping other musical attributes. This suggests a natural formulation for generative cover synthesis with pretrained music language models: explicitly control tonal content, while specifying lyrics and style through text. Existing approaches condition on frame-level features, tightly coupling generation to the reference's timing and structure, and limiting flexibility such as tempo variation, structural rearrangement, or partial conditioning. To this end, we present MuLaCover, a cover generation model that conditions a pretrained text-to-song foundation model on an editable symbolic lead sheet. Our design enables alignment-free control: generated outputs preserve the tonal signature of the source without frame-level alignment, allowing flexible timing, structure, and segment-level generation. We further introduce a training curriculum with partially mismatched audio-symbolic pairs, improving diversity and robustness. We evaluate MuLaCover with objective metrics, standard subjective ratings, and in-depth expert interviews that provide fine-grained diagnostic insights. Experiments show that MuLaCover achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source systems and is competitive with leading commercial models such as Suno-v5.5. Audio samples and code are available at our project page: https://mulalabs.ai/mulacover/

papers.title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
papers.authors: Kanglin Xu, Yash Kurkure, Yihe Zhang, Michael E. Papka et al.
papers.summary: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.

papers.title: SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling
papers.authors: Kanglin Xu, Michael Papka, Zhiling Lan
papers.summary: In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. However, these estimates are notoriously inaccurate, as users tend to overestimate walltime to prevent the scheduler from terminating their jobs prematurely. While existing work on learning-based walltime prediction primarily focuses on maximizing prediction accuracy, such predictions are inherently risky for walltime recommendations. Specifically, underestimation leads to job termination before completion, resulting in lost progress and wasted resources. In this study, we present SafeWall, a novel recommendation method that adjusts walltime predictions by incorporating an explicit, nonnegative safety buffer to mitigate underestimation risk. The core of our approach is a risk-aware buffer that dynamically calibrates safety margins based on individual user's historical behavior. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. We evaluate SafeWall using five public workload traces, including the full-lifetime job log from the 4,392-node Theta machine at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Across all traces, SafeWall substantially reduces underestimation risk compared to the unbuffered base predictors, while preserving competitive accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SPEAR-UIC/JSSPP26-SafeWall.

papers.title: Point2Acoustic: Efficient Room Acoustic Parameter Estimation from 3D Geometry and Material Properties
papers.authors: Xun Gao, Raksha Ramakrishna, Tommy Falk, Werner de Bruijn
papers.summary: Scene-adaptive immersive audio rendering requires rapid estimation of acoustic parameters that reflect the surrounding environment. For repeated runtime scene updates, performing a detailed geometric-acoustic simulation for every update can be computationally costly. We present Point2Acoustic, a learning-based framework for direct estimation of six-band reverberation time (RT₆₀) and reverberant-to-direct ratio (RDR) from 3D scene geometry and acoustic material properties. Each scene is represented by a surface-sampled point cloud with spatial coordinates and frequency-dependent absorption and scattering coefficients, and encoded using PointNet or PointNet++. We train and evaluate the framework on a synthetic furnished-room dataset with varied geometry and acoustic materials, using geometric-acoustic simulation to obtain reference targets. Point2Acoustic achieves accurate multi-band prediction with millisecond-scale inference, and ablation results indicate that explicit global room descriptors and semantic surface labels provide no consistent benefit. The proposed formulation supports efficient scene-adaptive acoustic rendering in extended reality (XR).

papers.title: Label Authority in Speech Emotion Recognition: Intended and Perceived Ground Truth in Emozionalmente
papers.authors: Marco Giordano, Stefano Giacomelli, Claudia Rinaldi, Fabio Graziosi
papers.summary: Ground truth in Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is often presented as a single categorical fact, yet an acted emotion and the emotion heard by listeners describe different aspects of the same recording. We examine this distinction in Emozionalmente, an acted Italian corpus that provides both an elicited production label and five listener judgements for every clip. Using frozen XLS-R, HuBERT, and WavLM representations with matched probes, we compare three label authorities: the expressed condition, the listeners' hard plurality, and their complete vote distribution. The results tell a consistent story. Recovering the expressed condition is easier than predicting a tie-broken listener plurality, but that gap compares two different questions rather than revealing a general loss of SER ability. As listener agreement weakens, the plurality becomes an increasingly brittle hard target. Training on the full vote distribution does not substantially change which class wins the model's hard decision, but it produces probability assignments that more closely follow the alternatives selected by listeners, especially for ambiguous clips. No authority therefore replaces the others. Expressed labels describe how speech was produced, pluralities provide an operational single-class decision, and vote distributions preserve perceptual uncertainty. For human-facing Internet of Sounds applications, evaluations should state which authority is being predicted, retain its aggregation rule and agreement information, and use distributional scores when disagreement is part of the target.

papers.title: Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines: From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
papers.authors: Thomas George, Severin A. T. Klapproth, Jens Henrik Göbbert, Jonathan Windgassen et al.
papers.summary: In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

papers.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
papers.authors: Zixuan Dong, Yanghai Wang, Hanyan Bian, Jiaxi Tao et al.
papers.summary: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.
